First - for clarification - I define "censorship" as actions taken by a third party in order to prevent a speaker/writer from reaching a potential audience in the first place.

Downvoting is self-evidently at least an attempt at censorship. It isn't specifically censorship in and of itself, since it requires more than a single downvote in order to interfere with the writer's attempt to communicate to an audience. That's what makes it seem legitimate - because it requires a particular threshold of cumulative downvotes in order to successfully censor the message, those so inclined can pretend that that somehow makes it something other than censorship, because, after all, they don't have the power to censor all by themselves, right? They have to have other people agree with them first. So it's just the "community" reflecting its "standards."

Nonetheless, the clear intent is to interfere in order to try to prevent a writer from reaching a potential audience, and that's censorship.

Upvoting is a bit more nuanced, and I'm not sure that it could be considered censorship, really. Yes - it is true that upvoting lifts things to the top of the page, so necessarily it pushes other things to the bottom of the page, and those things at the bottom of the page are less likely to be read, but I don't quite count it as censorship because that's not the intent. The intent is to get people to read the thing that's being upvoted - not to prevent them from reading the things that merely aren't being upvoted. The intent of downvoting is specifically to try to prevent people from reading the thing that's being downvoted.

To your questions, if voting was merely recorded and had no bearing on whether or not a post is displayed, then voting would merely be an exercise of free speech - a simple tally of the number of people who like or dislike a given post. But since voting has a direct effect on whether or not the post is displayed at all, it goes beyond mere free speech.

And anyone who acts to prevent another from being able to reach an audience at all is censoring. It's easier for authorities to do it since they have a monopoly on nominally legitimate violence - a private citizen censor risks a punch in the mouth, while an officially empowered censor can have you arrested for refusing to abide by his authority. But either can successfully prevent another from being able to reach an audience, so either can censor.
